Cut Vinyl Decal Build and Apply

A cut vinyl decal goes onto a clean, dry surface under firm squeegee pressure. Avery Dennison's instructions call for squeegeeing before and after the application tape is peeled away, with extra attention to the edges.

At a glance

Layers shown
Transfer tape, vinyl film, adhesive and substrate
Surface
Cleaned and completely dry
Squeegee strokes
Firm, short and overlapping, from the top center downward and outward
Tape removal
Peeled back from a corner at a 180° angle
After the tape
Squeegee again with very firm pressure, including all edges
Source of the steps
Avery Dennison's application bulletin for its films

The layers and the surface

The infographic shows a decal as a stack. From the top down it labels transfer tape, vinyl film, adhesive and the substrate, which is the surface the decal goes on. It gives painted aluminum, acrylic and glass as examples of suitable substrates.

Avery Dennison's application bulletin for its films says every application surface must be considered contaminated and must be cleaned, and that the surface must be completely dry. On a painted surface, the drying or curing period of the paint system must be followed. The bulletin warns that failing to do so can result in poor decal performance and difficult removal. It also directs the applicator to the film's product data bulletin for recommended substrates and for minimum and maximum application temperatures.

Sources: [1]

Hinge, peel and squeegee

The infographic lays out the work as a strip of steps: clean, hinge, peel, squeegee, remove and check edges. The bulletin's own step-by-step procedure uses a top hinge. Once the decal is in position, a masking tape hinge is applied along its top edge. The decal is then flipped up over the hinge and the liner is removed.

The bulletin says to squeegee from the top center downward and outward, with firm, short, overlapping strokes. The infographic's squeegee panel gives a similar instruction: firm, overlapping strokes from the center outward. Avery Dennison says not to use application fluid, the so-called wet method. Water or fluid that is not squeezed out can remain between the surface and the decal and reduce its ultimate adhesion.

Sources: [1]

Removing the tape and checking edges

Application pressure helps seat the adhesive. Avery Dennison recommends squeegeeing the decal before the premask is removed and again afterward. The premask, which the bulletin also calls application tape, comes off by peeling back a corner and pulling it back at a 180° angle. The infographic labels this tape transfer tape. The second squeegee pass is aimed particularly at edges that could lift as the tape peels away. The bulletin calls for very firm squeegee pressure over the entire decal, including all edges.

Any air bubbles are punctured with a straight pin and squeegeed from the edge of the bubble toward the puncture. The infographic shows an air-release path as well, with a caption that says air escapes through tiny channels in the adhesive when pressure is applied. Its last step is to check edges. It contrasts a good seal with edge lift and states that edge lift can lead to moisture, dirt and premature failure.

Sources: [1]

How a Thermal Receipt Fades

Direct thermal receipt paper carries a heat-sensitive coating of dye and developer that forms marks when heated. The print can fade in sunlight or under prolonged fluorescent light, and plasticizers in some tapes and sleeves can fade it as well.

At a glance

How the mark forms
Heat activates a dye and developer coating
Color starts to develop
Between 60 °C and 100 °C, depending on the grade (Jujo Thermal papers)
Fades in
Direct sunlight and prolonged fluorescent light
Also fades with
Plasticizers in PVC film and some tapes, and sweat
Long-term storage
In the dark, below 25 °C, relative humidity below 65%
Recommended files
Polyolefin or polyester

How the mark is made

Direct thermal paper uses a heat-sensitive coating of dye and developer. The infographic shows the paper in cross-section: base paper fibers at the bottom, a thermal coating that holds a colorless dye and a developer, and a protective top coat. Its caption says no ink or toner is used, and that heat triggers a reaction in the coating that turns it dark. A second panel shows the heat elements of a thermal print head in contact with the paper as a dark mark forms.

Jujo Thermal, a maker of thermal paper, gives figures for its own papers. They begin to develop color at temperatures between 60 °C and 100 °C and reach what the company calls an applicable density at 70 to 120 °C, depending on the grade. The paper also shows similar signs of development at high temperature or in high humidity. Frictional heat from scratching, or pressure from hard metal objects or fingernails, causes an image to develop too.

Sources: [1]

What fades the print

The manufacturer says the printed image tends to fade in direct sunlight, and that it also shows a tendency to fade under conventional fluorescent light over prolonged periods. For that reason it advises filing printed paper soon after printing. All papers turn yellow with time, especially in direct sunlight for prolonged periods.

The storage material matters as well as the light. PVC film contains plasticizer, and prolonged contact with it reduces the paper's image-forming property and fades the printed image. Plasticizers in some tapes can fade the print as well, and so can sweat. Adhesives that contain volatile organic solvents, such as alcohols, esters and ketones, cause color formation in the paper.

The infographic groups the causes of fading as heat, sunlight and UV, abrasion, hand oils, plasticizers from some plastics, solvents and cleaners, and humidity or poor storage. It shows a receipt going from fresh to fading to aged and discolored, and describes fading as gradual and irreversible.

Sources: [1]

Keeping a receipt legible

For long-term storage, the manufacturer says its papers should be kept in the dark, at an average ambient temperature of less than 25 °C and a relative humidity of less than 65%. For files and cases it recommends polyolefins or polyester.

The infographic's storage panel gives similar general advice: keep receipts cool, dry and dark, and keep them apart from vinyl or plastic sleeves and chemicals. It suggests paper folders or envelopes, and scanning or photographing important receipts to keep a digital copy.

Sources: [1]

Planted Aquarium Nitrogen Cycle

In an aquarium, bacteria turn the ammonia that fish produce into nitrite and then into nitrate. The process needs oxygen, and making nitrate does not mean the nitrogen has left the aquarium.

At a glance

Process
Nitrification, in two biological steps
Step one
Bacteria oxidize ammonia to nitrite
Step two
Other bacteria oxidize nitrite to nitrate
What it needs
Oxygen, and a biological filter where the bacteria can colonize
New biofilter
Six to eight weeks to build up enough bacteria
Nitrate removal
Water changes or separate denitrification systems

Where the ammonia comes from

Ammonia is the primary waste product of fish metabolism. A University of Florida IFAS Extension publication on ammonia says most of it leaves a fish by diffusion through the gills. The decay of uneaten feed and other organic matter adds more, but in most aquaculture or hobbyist systems the digestion of the feed the fish eat is the primary source. The infographic puts it differently: fish waste and uneaten food break down and release ammonia into the water.

Ammonia is colorless and, even at levels toxic to fish, odorless, so the only way to know it is present is to test the water. In water it exists in two forms, un-ionized ammonia and ionized ammonium. The un-ionized form is approximately 100 times more toxic to fish. In healthy ponds and tanks, the publication says, ammonia levels should always be zero.

Sources: [1]

Two steps, two groups of bacteria

Nitrification happens in two biological steps. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria, including Nitrosospira and Nitrosomonas, convert ammonia to nitrite. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria, including Nitrospira and Nitrobacter, convert nitrite to nitrate, which is much less toxic. The infographic labels both groups as beneficial bacteria.

Both groups need oxygen. If oxygen levels are not sufficient, the bacteria can stop functioning or die, and ammonia and nitrite levels increase. In tanks and aquariums, the publication says, a biological filter must be provided as a place where the bacteria can colonize. A new biofilter requires six to eight weeks to build up enough bacteria to reduce ammonia and nitrite effectively.

Sources: [1]

Where the nitrate goes

Making nitrate does not mean nitrogen has left the aquarium. The publication says that in natural systems and ponds, plants take up nitrate as a fertilizer, so levels typically remain low. In closed systems with little or no water exchange, nitrate can accumulate, and water changes or separate denitrification systems are needed to remove it.

The infographic shows both routes in a planted freshwater tank. It states that plants use nitrate and ammonium for growth, that roots absorb nutrients such as ammonium and nitrate, and that regular water changes remove excess nitrate and other dissolved wastes. It also states that beneficial bacteria thrive around roots and in the substrate, and that root surfaces release natural compounds that feed them. These root-zone details appear on the infographic, not in the extension publication.

Sources: [1]

Keeping the cycle steady

The infographic closes with care guidance: test water regularly, avoid overfeeding, and add plants gradually so the aquarium can adjust and stay balanced. The extension publication supports the first two. It says testing is the only way to know ammonia is present and that overfeeding is a major cause of high ammonia concentrations. The advice about adding plants appears only on the infographic.

Sources: [1]

These are the notes the picture was checked against. Some are written as instructions to the illustrator.

  • Nitrification happens in two biological steps: ammonia is oxidized to nitrite, then nitrite is oxidized to nitrate. It requires oxygen; nitrate production does not mean nitrogen has left the aquarium. [1]

How a Mechanical Fire Sprinkler Head Works

An automatic fire sprinkler head is held closed by a heat-responsive element, normally a liquid-filled glass bulb. When a fire heats the head to its operating temperature, the element breaks or releases and water sprays out over the fire.

At a glance

Held closed by
A heat-responsive element pressing on a sealing mechanism
Usual element
Liquid-filled glass bulb; other heads use a fusible metal link
Opens when
The head reaches its predetermined operating temperature
Which heads open
Only those closest to the fire
Water spread by
A deflector
Example rating
68 °C (155 °F), red bulb filling

Parts of the head

The infographic shows a cutaway of a typical head with its parts labeled: the frame, the threaded inlet that connects to the sprinkler pipe, the heat-sensitive element, a compression screw, a cap or plug, the seat and orifice, and the deflector plate.

In normal conditions, according to the British Automatic Fire Sprinkler Association, the heat-responsive element holds the waterway of the head closed by applying pressure to a sealing mechanism. The element is normally a liquid-filled glass bulb. Other heads use a fusible metal link in its place. The association's table of operating temperature ratings matches each rating to a color of bulb filling, from 57 °C (orange) to 182 °C (mauve). A bulb rated 68 °C (155 °F) has a red filling.

Sources: [1]

What happens in a fire

Sprinkler heads are spaced on or close to the ceiling, where heat collects as it rises during a fire. Each head operates only when it reaches its predetermined operating temperature. The element then breaks apart or releases, and water pressure in the sprinkler piping overcomes the sealing mechanism and sprays water on the fire. The infographic shows this as a sequence: standby with the orifice sealed, heat releasing the element so the plug drops away, then water flowing through the orifice.

The water is distributed by a deflector over the location of the fire. The infographic shows the stream striking the deflector plate and breaking into droplets that spread below the ceiling. Besides extinguishing or controlling the fire, the association says, the water helps to cool the hot gases produced and pre-wets areas immediately next to the fire to inhibit fire growth.

Sources: [1]

Only the heads near the fire open

Sprinklers operate independently of one another, so only those closest to the fire open. Sprinklers in areas where there is no fire remain closed and do not release water. The infographic makes the same point with a ceiling of several heads, one of them spraying over a fire. Its caption says heat must reach the element to activate it, and unexposed heads remain closed.

Sources: [1]

Corrosion, paint, damage and cover plates

The infographic lists visual clues that a head may have a problem: corrosion, paint blockage, bent or damaged parts, and a missing cover plate. Its captions say rust or corrosion can weaken components, paint can interfere with operation or hide damage, and physical damage can prevent proper operation.

The association notes that the air or water inside sprinkler piping may be corrosive, so the sprinkler frame must be made of materials that resist that corrosion, even after many years in the field. It also describes concealed sprinklers, which sit flush with the ceiling behind a small metal disc. The disc is soldered to a support bracket. Heated in a fire, this melts and lets the disc fall away, exposing the sprinkler head.

Sources: [1]

How a Quartz Watch Keeps Time --slot factual-infographic

A quartz watch keeps time by a quartz crystal that oscillates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied. A frequency of 32,768 Hz became the standard, though the first quartz wristwatch used 8,192 Hz.

At a glance

Timing element
A quartz crystal oscillating at a precise frequency under an applied voltage
Standard frequency
32,768 Hz in later quartz timepieces
First quartz wristwatch
Seiko Quartz Astron 35SQ, launched December 25, 1969
Astron's frequency
8,192 Hz
Astron's accuracy
±0.2 seconds per day, ±5 seconds per month

The crystal sets the pace

A quartz timepiece uses a property of a quartz crystal: it oscillates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied to it. That frequency serves as the standard for keeping time, in place of the pendulum or balance wheel of conventional timepieces. The Seiko Museum Ginza says the change increased the precision of timepieces dramatically.

The first Seiko Quartz Astron contained a quartz oscillator with a vibration frequency of 8,192 Hz. A frequency of 32,768 Hz became the standard for later quartz timepieces, so not every early quartz watch used the same frequency. The infographic labels 32,768 Hz as a typical quartz oscillator and states that the crystal vibrates that many times per second.

The infographic adds that the performance of a quartz watch can be influenced by temperature, battery condition, magnetism, shock, moisture and aging.

Sources: [1]

From battery to hands

The infographic lays out the signal path in a battery-powered watch with hands. Battery power feeds an oscillator circuit, the quartz crystal vibrates, the timing pulses are divided, a stepper motor advances, and the gear train moves the hands. Its cutaway labels the coin cell battery, integrated circuit, quartz tuning-fork crystal can, stepper motor coil and gear train, along with the dial, hands, crown, case, gasket and caseback.

Several of these parts appear in the museum's account of Seiko's quartz watches. It lists a miniature, low-power, shock-resistant quartz oscillator of the tuning-fork type, a second hand that ticks once per second to save power, and an open-type stepping motor that allowed a space-saving arrangement of the coil, stator and rotor. The museum says the use of these technologies in Seiko's watches made them the global standard.

Sources: [1]

How quartz reached the wrist

The quartz clock was invented in America by Warren Marrison in 1927. Bulova launched a tuning fork watch in 1960 that vibrated at 360 Hz and was accurate to within two seconds per day. The museum says the pursuit of even higher precision led to quartz watches.

On December 25, 1969, Seiko launched the Seiko Quartz Astron 35SQ, which the museum describes as the world's first quartz wristwatch. Its accuracy was ±0.2 seconds per day and ±5 seconds per month, at a time when a few seconds to a few dozen seconds per day was considered normal for high-precision mechanical wristwatches.

Sources: [1]

How a Honeybee Waggle Dance Shares a Food Location

The waggle dance is how a honey bee forager tells her nestmates where to find food. The angle of her straight run gives the direction relative to the sun, and the time she spends waggling gives the distance.

At a glance

Who dances
A forager back at the colony with nectar or pollen
Where
On the surface of the wax comb
Used for food
More than 150 meters from the hive
Direction
The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical
Distance
The duration of the waggle run; longer for farther food

When a forager dances

NC State Extension describes the dance as something an experienced forager most often does when she returns to her colony with a load of food, either nectar or pollen. If the food is good enough, she will often dance on the surface of the wax comb. Returning foragers use the dance to recruit nestmates to the food.

The waggle dance is the form performed by bees foraging at food sources more than 150 meters from the hive. It passes on two things: direction and distance.

Sources: [1]

The shape of the dance

The dancer runs straight ahead for a short distance, returns in a semicircle to her starting point, runs the straight course again, and then makes a semicircle in the opposite direction. That completes a full figure-eight circuit. During the straight run her body, especially the abdomen, wags vigorously from side to side.

The infographic shows this on a patch of comb. One bee stands on a straight line labeled waggle run, curved arrows beside it are labeled return loop, and a row of other bees faces her at close range.

Sources: [1]

Reading direction and distance

Direction comes from the angle of the waggle run. The angle the bee takes relative to vertical on the comb represents the angle to the flowers relative to the direction of the sun outside. The infographic's sun angle panel draws the outdoor half of that relationship, with a hive, the sun and a line labeled food direction.

Distance comes from time. As the distance to the food increases, the waggle run lasts longer, and the extension publication calls the duration of the straight run the simplest and most reliable indicator of distance. The infographic's distance cue panel reads: shorter, less vigorous waggle run for closer food, and longer, more vigorous waggle run for farther food.

Sources: [1]

Scent finishes the search

According to NC State Extension, the most commonly accepted view is that recruits go to the area the dance describes and then home in on the flower patch using odor cues. Around its main scene the infographic adds a nectar source panel, a cutaway labeled hive context, and close-ups of wax cells, pollen grains, antennae and wing veins.

Sources: [1]

How a Bicycle Freehub Body Engages and Coasts

A freehub is the ratcheting mechanism on the rear hub of most modern derailleur bikes. Its pawls lock onto ratchet teeth when the rider pedals and let the wheel turn independently of the cassette while coasting.

At a glance

What it is
The ratcheting mechanism attached to the rear hub
Holds
The cassette cogs, on a splined cylinder
Inside
Bearings and a clutch system, usually ratcheting teeth and pawls
Pedaling
Pawls engage the ratchet teeth so the cassette drives the hub
Coasting
The wheel turns independently of the cassette
Usual lubricant
Liquid lubricant, recommended by most manufacturers

What the freehub is

The freehub is the ratcheting mechanism attached to the rear hub of most modern derailleur bikes. It uses a splined cylinder to hold the cassette cogs. The cogs themselves have no moving parts. All the moving parts are in the freehub body, which contains bearings and a clutch system, usually ratcheting teeth and pawls.

The infographic's cutaway labels the hub shell, pawls, cassette splines, bearing, axle, seal and ratchet teeth. A second strip sets the internal parts out in order: cassette body, pawls, springs, ratchet ring, bearing, seal, axle end cap and hub shell.

Sources: [1]

Pedaling and coasting

In a typical pawl-and-ratchet freehub, pedaling makes the pawls engage the ratchet teeth, so the cassette can drive the hub. While coasting, the wheel turns independently of the cassette. The infographic draws the two states one above the other, as a pedaling load path and a coasting click path.

Park Tool's service guide notes that the freehub's pawls and bearings operate only while the bike is coasting, when there is very little load or stress on the freehub. When the bike is pedaled, the pawls lock onto the ratcheting teeth and the freehub bearings take very little stress.

The guide also describes a different clutch. In the DT-Hugi design, the clutch is made up of two star ratchet gears whose angled teeth face one another, each pushed by a spring.

Sources: [1]

Lubrication and wear

Because the internal parts see so little load, Park Tool says bicycle grease is typically not required inside a freehub, and most manufacturers recommend a liquid lubricant. Some of its brand-specific procedures do call for grease on particular parts. For Campagnolo freehubs, for example, the springs and pawls are greased before they are installed.

With enough use a freehub wears out. The pawls may begin to slip and the bearings may become rough. If cleaning and lubricating does not resolve slipping, sticking or noise, the guide says to replace the freehub unit with a new one. The infographic's wear check shows a worn pawl tip, dry and dirty grease, and a contaminated seal as examples. It also lists materials: hardened steel for the pawls and ratchet, aluminum for the hub shell, bearing steel, a rubber seal and grease for lubrication.

Sources: [1]

How a Refrigerator Door Seal Works

A refrigerator door seal is a flexible gasket that includes a magnetic strip. The gasket closes the gap around the door by compressing against the cabinet, which limits warm-air leaks.

At a glance

Seal type
Flexible magnetic door gasket
Magnet
An extruded magnetic strip shaped for the gasket
Gasket's job
Closing the gap around the door
Strips also used in
Water bars, tea bar machines, upright freezers and medical freezers
Maker's stated purpose
Insulation, freshness and preventing cold leakage

The gasket and its magnetic strip

A magnetic refrigerator seal can use an extruded magnetic strip shaped for the door gasket. The strip is one part of the seal. The gasket is the material that closes the gap around the door.

HIGA Magnetic Materials, which makes such strips, offers them with cross-sections and pole layouts made to order. The company says it developed extrusion screw materials for magnetic granules, for efficient extrusion, and that its own magnetizing fixtures and magnetic circuit design improve magnetic performance. It lists the strips as used in magnetic door seals for refrigerators, water bars, tea bar machines, upright freezers and medical freezers.

The infographic's cutaway labels the parts at the door edge: the cabinet frame, a flexible vinyl gasket with a hollow compression chamber, the embedded magnetic strip, the contact surface, the door liner and the metal door shell.

Sources: [1]

How the seal closes and leaks

HIGA describes the job of a magnetic door seal as providing insulation and freshness and preventing cold leakage. The infographic shows two actions behind that. The flexible gasket compresses against the cabinet to form a seal, and in a step labeled magnetic pull-in, the magnet pulls the gasket tightly to the steel face. Arrows mark cold air staying in and warm air staying out.

A gasket that is dirty, twisted or poorly seated can let warm air leak in and can develop a condensation risk. The infographic shows gaps letting warm air in and cold air out, with moisture forming on warm surfaces near the leaks. It contrasts a good continuous contact line, with even pressure all the way around, with a wavy or damaged corner where gaps cause leaks.

A care panel on the infographic shows inspecting the entire seal with a light, cleaning with mild soap and water, using nonmetal tools to avoid cutting or tearing the gasket, and drying and reseating it so it is fully seated all the way around.

How a Manual Can Opener Works

A handheld rotary can opener clamps onto the rim of a can, feeds itself around and cuts the lid. A 1931 patent describes the arrangement: a cutter wheel and a feed wheel on two pivoted levers, geared together.

At a glance

Patent
US1838525A, granted December 29, 1931
Inventor
Charles Arthur Bunker
Main parts
Two pivoted levers with handles, a cutter, a feed wheel and gears
Where it cuts
Through the can end, inward of the seam, not through the side wall
What guides it
The can rim, held between the two wheels

The parts

The patent, granted to Charles Arthur Bunker on December 29, 1931, describes a pair of levers pivoted on a plate, each with a handle. A cutter is mounted so it can rotate on one lever, and a feed member on the other, in alignment with it. The cutter is beveled. Gears on the cutter and feeder mesh when the handles are moved toward each other.

The infographic shows a handheld rotary opener with similar parts. Its cutaway labels two handles, a hinge, a turning knob, a drive gear, a serrated feed wheel, a hardened cutting wheel, axle pins and rivets, with the can lid and rim in cross-section beneath.

Sources: [1]

Clamping onto the rim

In the patent's account, the handles are first spread to separate the cutter and the feed wheel. The bead of the can, also called the chime, goes between them, with the cutter on the inner side of the can wall. Closing the handles makes the feed wheel engage the lower edge of the bead and forces the cutter into and through the top of the can.

The infographic's sequence starts the same way: open jaws approach the rim, then the handles squeeze to seat the wheels.

Sources: [1]

Cutting around the lid

Once the can end is pierced, turning the crank handle rotates the cutter, and the cutter and feed wheel travel around the bead formed by the can's seam. The rim guides the opener while the cutting wheel moves along the inside edge, and the wheels keep the opener positioned so the cutter can make a continuous cut around the top. The feed wheel bears on the outer wall of the can and the lower edge of the bead.

One stated purpose of the patent concerns where the cut is made: through the end of the can, inward of the seam between the end and the side wall, instead of through the side wall as had been done before. Its cutter also turns the cut edge downward against the body of the can. The infographic shows the last step differently, with the cutting wheel shearing the lid while the lid edge lifts.

The infographic's comparison panel shows good contact, with the feed wheel and cutting wheel tracking smoothly on the rim, beside two problem signs: wheels that are not aligned, so one side digs in, and a dull or damaged wheel that skips on the rim and leaves marks.

Sources: [1]

How a Zipper Slider Interlocks Teeth

A zipper has three main components: two rows of meshing elements, a slider and fabric tape. The slider, which has a Y-shaped tunnel inside, brings the elements together so they mesh when moved one way and separates them when moved the other.

At a glance

Components
Elements, slider and tape
Elements
The component with teeth that mesh with each other
Slider
Moved by hand; has a Y-shaped tunnel inside
Tape
The fabric component
Element precision
Within one hundredth of a millimeter, according to YKK

Three components

YKK, a zipper maker, divides a zipper broadly into three components. The elements are the component with teeth that mesh with each other, and they run in two matching rows. The slider is the component moved by the user's hand. The tape is the fabric component.

The infographic's exploded view labels more pieces: the slider body and pull tab, a top stop and a bottom stop, the zipper tape, coil or molded teeth, stitching and the fabric edge. Its materials panel shows a brass or plated metal slider, nylon coil and polyester tape.

Sources: [1]

Inside the slider

YKK calls the slider the key to opening and closing. It has a Y-shaped tunnel inside. Pulling the slider up causes the elements to mesh, closing the zipper. Pulling it down widens the gap between the meshing elements and opens the zipper. The uneven sections on the left and right elements mesh together like gears.

The infographic shows closing as a sequence: separated teeth enter the slider, the channel guides them together, the teeth interlock, and a closed chain exits at the bottom. Its cutaway labels the slider's pull tab, crown, throat, Y-shaped channel and bottom exit.

Sources: [1]

Why shape and size matter

Smooth opening and closing depends heavily on the shape and dimensions of each component, YKK says. If there is a measurement error in the elements, the zipper will not open properly, and a zipper that should be closed will come open from the center. Making the elements requires high precision, to within one hundredth of a millimeter.

The infographic's comparison panel shows good alignment beside two faults, skipped teeth and a loose slider. Its close-up panel points to a worn slider channel, a bent tooth and frayed fabric.

Sources: [1]
